medium.resumo: AI Has Built the Infrastructure. Now It Has to Build the Economy.
medium.conteudo_html:
Most Significant Post Of The Day-3 October 2026

AI Has Built the Infrastructure. Now It Has to Build the Economy.

The next phase of the AI boom depends less on bigger data centres and more on whether useful applications can generate enough value to justify them.

Source post: Reuters — AI’s race to transform the world before the money runs out

Why this development deserves a full article

The most significant AI story today is not a new model, product launch or safety incident. It is a harder question about the economics underneath the entire AI boom: can the industry create enough real value before the cost of building the infrastructure overwhelms the business case?

Reuters brought that question into sharp focus on 3 October with an analysis of the extraordinary sums now being committed to artificial intelligence. PwC projects global data-centre capital spending of about $31.6 trillion through 2050. Bain & Company estimates that annual AI infrastructure spending could reach $1.5 trillion by 2031, which would require an AI market approaching $6 trillion a year if capital expenditure remained around one quarter of sector revenue. Bain believes known consumer and enterprise uses might provide only $1.2 trillion to $1.8 trillion of that total, leaving roughly $4.2 trillion to be found from new sources of value.

Those figures are forecasts, not facts about what will definitely happen. They depend on adoption rates, prices, energy availability, chip costs and new applications that may or may not emerge. Even so, the direction of travel is clear. The AI sector is moving from a software story into an infrastructure, financing and productivity story. That matters for businesses, governments, universities and public services because the economics of the underlying market will eventually influence pricing, procurement, supplier stability and where AI capability is concentrated.

What has happened

Investment in AI infrastructure has accelerated dramatically. Hyperscalers and model developers are committing large sums to chips, networking, data centres, energy and long-term compute contracts. Bain estimates that capital expenditure by Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta and Oracle could reach about $780 billion in 2026. It also expects annual AI infrastructure spending to rise towards $1.5 trillion by 2031.

PwC takes an even longer view. Its 2026 Global Data Centre Outlook projects $31.6 trillion of data-centre capital expenditure through 2050 in its central scenario. The firm also says spending would not be a one-off construction wave. Servers, GPUs and related equipment need repeated replacement, which means the investment cycle could continue for decades. PwC estimates annual data-centre capital spending could rise from roughly $800 billion in 2026 to $1.8 trillion by 2050.

The scale is illustrated by Anthropic. The company says its annualised revenue run rate has exceeded $30 billion, but Reuters reported from its IPO prospectus that Anthropic expects to spend at least $518 billion on infrastructure over a decade. That does not mean the company must fund that entire amount immediately, nor does it prove the spending will be uneconomic. It does show how much capital leading AI companies believe they will need to remain competitive.

The central issue is not whether AI is useful

There is already strong evidence that AI can save time and improve performance in specific tasks. Software development, document drafting, customer support, research, translation and data analysis are all areas where organisations are reporting practical benefits. The difficulty is moving from useful applications to an economy large enough to support the infrastructure now being built.

Bain’s analysis is helpful because it separates existing value from the additional value still required. The consultancy estimates that consumer AI products could generate between $200 billion and $400 billion a year by 2031. Enterprise adoption could add another $1 trillion to $1.4 trillion in provider revenue as companies use AI in software development, sales, marketing, customer service and IT operations.

Those are already very large markets. Yet Bain’s model still leaves a gap of about $4.2 trillion if the sector is to support $1.5 trillion of annual capital expenditure on conventional commercial ratios. Its conclusion is that productivity improvements inside today’s business processes will not be enough on their own. Entirely new markets will have to emerge.

This is the key point. The next stage of AI may have to create new economic activity rather than merely reduce the cost of existing work.

Where could the missing value come from?

Bain identifies several possible sources. One is advertising and search, where AI interfaces could capture part of the money currently spent on conventional web search and digital advertising. Bain estimates this could contribute around $100 billion to $200 billion.

A second area is what it calls autonomous everything: AI controlling cars, trucks, drones and industrial equipment. Bain sees a possible $400 billion opportunity here. A third is physical AI, including robotics, simulations and digital twins used in manufacturing, engineering and other parts of the physical economy. Bain estimates that category could represent about $900 billion.

The remaining opportunity is less defined. It could include AI-assisted drug discovery, new materials, scientific research, healthcare services or products that do not yet exist. This is where the argument becomes more speculative. The potential may be very large, but it cannot yet be treated as established future revenue.

History provides both encouragement and caution. Railways, electrification and the internet created enormous long-term value, but the infrastructure was often built before reliable business models existed. Some investors lost heavily even though society eventually benefited. A technology can transform the economy while many individual companies, projects or financing structures fail along the way.

Financing makes the timing problem more important

The economics are becoming more sensitive because an increasing share of AI investment is being financed through debt and long-term contractual commitments. The Bank for International Settlements has documented a shift from funding AI investment mainly through operating cash flow towards corporate debt, private credit and off-balance-sheet structures.

The BIS describes arrangements in which special-purpose vehicles build or acquire data-centre assets using outside debt, while technology companies sign long-term leases or capacity agreements. Economically, these can behave like borrowing even when much of the debt does not sit directly on the hyperscaler’s balance sheet.

This matters because technological potential and financial timing are not the same thing. AI could prove transformational over twenty years, while a particular data centre or financing vehicle still struggles to meet obligations over the next five. Debt has repayment schedules. Equipment depreciates. Chips become obsolete. Energy and construction costs can change.

The gap between long-term technological promise and shorter-term financial commitments is therefore one of the most important risks to watch.

Productivity is the unresolved test

The investment case ultimately depends on productivity and revenue. If AI enables companies to produce more, create better products and open new markets, the infrastructure can support sustained economic growth. If most benefits remain small efficiency gains, the numbers become much harder to justify.

Reuters cited JPMorgan analysis saying broad-based US productivity gains remain difficult to identify at the scale required by current valuations. The article also noted that past general-purpose technologies often took many years, sometimes decades, to produce their full productivity effect.

That historical lag creates a difficult comparison. Financial markets and technology companies can build infrastructure quickly. Organisational change is slower. Businesses need to redesign processes, retrain staff, alter controls, integrate systems and sometimes change the way they sell products. Public services face procurement, assurance and regulatory constraints on top of that.

In other words, the technology may improve faster than institutions can absorb it. That does not make the technology unsuccessful. It can still make the investment cycle volatile.

What this means for enterprise AI strategy

For senior leaders, the practical lesson is not to stop investing in AI. It is to separate the industry-wide investment story from the organisation’s own business case.

A company does not need AI to generate trillions of dollars of new global revenue in order to justify a well-designed internal use case. It needs a credible local return. That may come from reduced handling time, higher sales conversion, better customer service, lower error rates, faster software delivery or improved decision support.

However, organisations should avoid assuming that falling model prices or abundant compute will continue indefinitely. If the sector’s infrastructure economics tighten, suppliers may change pricing, reduce subsidies, bundle services differently or prioritise customers with higher margins.

Business cases should therefore test more than the current subscription price. They should model usage growth, token or compute costs, integration costs, governance overhead and the possibility of switching supplier. The most resilient AI programmes will be those that still make sense under less generous market conditions.

Implications for procurement and supplier assurance

Procurement teams should treat AI supplier resilience as part of technology risk. This does not mean trying to predict which model company will succeed. It means understanding material dependencies before they become operationally critical.

Key questions include whether the service depends on one cloud provider, whether prices are tied to underlying compute costs, what happens if a model is withdrawn, how easily workloads can move elsewhere and whether data can be exported in a usable form.

Long contracts may secure favourable pricing, but they can also lock an organisation into a rapidly changing market. Short contracts preserve flexibility but may provide less commercial certainty. There is no single correct answer. The important point is that the choice should be explicit rather than accidental.

Public-sector and Higher Education buyers should also pay attention to concentration. If a small number of frontier providers become deeply embedded across core services, supplier failure or sudden price changes could have effects well beyond one application.

A different perspective for the UK and Europe

The enormous US-led capital build-out may also create opportunities for regions that are not trying to match it directly. Europe has often been criticised for lagging the United States in frontier-model development and private AI investment. That remains a competitive weakness in some areas, but value may not accrue only to model builders.

If models become cheaper and more interchangeable, organisations that use them well could capture substantial economic benefit without owning the most expensive infrastructure. The critical capability would then be adoption: combining AI with strong data, redesigned processes, sector knowledge and effective governance.

For the UK, this suggests two parallel priorities. Strategic infrastructure matters, especially for research, national capability and public-sector resilience. But organisations also need the skills and operating models required to turn available AI into measurable productivity. Building data centres without adoption would waste capital. Buying AI licences without changing work would waste operating expenditure.

The two sides of the problem need to be managed together.

What leaders should consider now

Senior leaders should focus on five practical actions. First, require measurable business cases for scaled AI deployments rather than relying on general claims about future transformation. Second, distinguish pilot economics from production economics, especially where usage can grow rapidly. Third, identify supplier and infrastructure concentration before critical processes become dependent on a single provider. Fourth, invest in process redesign and workforce capability, because productivity gains rarely come from technology deployment alone. Fifth, keep strategic options open as model quality, pricing and infrastructure economics change.

For programme owners, this means setting benefits measures early and revisiting them after deployment. For technology teams, it means designing architectures that can accommodate more than one model where the additional complexity is justified. For procurement teams, it means negotiating portability and exit provisions. For policymakers, it means monitoring not only AI capability and safety, but also financing, energy demand, market concentration and the distribution of economic benefits.

The broader AI trend

This story strengthens a trend visible across recent AI briefings: the centre of gravity is moving from model capability to industrial economics.

Earlier phases of the AI boom were dominated by questions about which model could reason better, code better or handle more context. Those questions still matter, but they now sit inside a larger system of chips, energy, data centres, debt, cloud contracts and enterprise adoption.

The decisive competition may therefore be less about producing a single spectacular model and more about building an ecosystem that can turn intelligence into sustained economic value. That requires applications, distribution, trusted deployment, skilled users and viable infrastructure economics.

The companies that build the compute and the companies that create the value may not always be the same companies.

Conclusion

The central lesson of today’s story is straightforward. The AI industry has proved that it can attract capital and build infrastructure at extraordinary speed. It has not yet proved, at the same scale, that the applications needed to pay for that infrastructure will arrive quickly enough.

That is not an argument that AI will fail. Railways and the internet both went through periods in which investment expectations ran ahead of near-term returns, yet the infrastructure ultimately became economically indispensable. The same could happen with AI.

The important uncertainty is timing and distribution. Society may gain even if particular investors lose. Productivity may arrive even if some data centres are overbuilt. New markets may emerge, but not necessarily on the schedule assumed by today’s financing plans.

For organisations adopting AI, the practical response is to remain ambitious but disciplined. Focus on measurable value, retain flexibility, understand supplier dependencies and avoid confusing industry excitement with a local business case.

The next thing to watch is not simply how much more money is committed to AI. It is whether new applications begin to generate the revenue, productivity and economic growth required to support what has already been built.

AI Briefing Room Posts can be found here; https://aibriefingroom.online/

Key sources

Reuters — AI’s race to transform the world before the money runs out

Bain & Company — New Innovation Is Required to Fund AI’s $6 Trillion Buildout

PwC — Global investment in AI infrastructure to hit US$31.6 trillion through 2050

BIS — Financing the AI boom: from cash flows to debt

BIS — Financing the AI infrastructure boom: on- and off-balance sheet borrowing

Anthropic — Anthropic and Amazon expand compute collaboration

medium.titulo: Why LLM Streaming Works Locally and Breaks in Production
medium.resumo: The model is rarely at fault. The proxy, the closed tab, and the error that arrives after 200 OK are.
medium.conteudo_html:
The model is rarely at fault. The proxy, the closed tab, and the error that arrives after 200 OK are.

I’ve been working as an AI full-stack engineer for about two years. One thing I noticed early: almost every streaming tutorial ends at the same happy moment. You type a question, words appear one by one, and it feels like magic.

Then you put it behind real infrastructure, and the magic gets complicated. None of what breaks is an LLM problem. It lives in the plumbing between the model and the browser, and that plumbing rarely fits in a 30-line demo.

The most common break takes one command to prove. Reverse proxies like Nginx collect the upstream response and send it in bigger chunks by default, so your tokens sit in a buffer. Run curl -N against your production URL: if the answer arrives in one lump, something in front of your server is buffering it.

That is one of four ways it goes wrong:

  • The answer shows up all at once after ten seconds, instead of word by word.
  • A user closes the tab, and the server keeps generating (and you keep paying).
  • The stream dies halfway, and the UI shows half a sentence as if it were the full answer.
  • Some characters turn into �.

I want to be upfront about where this post comes from. I’m not writing as someone who has run streaming at a massive scale. I’m writing as someone who has built streaming features on real products, learned a lot of this by testing it and reading other engineers’ postmortems, and wishes someone had put it all in one place.

I’ll point out where I’m confident and where I’m still learning. If you’ve seen different behavior on your stack, I’d genuinely like to hear it.

The examples use Node/Express and the browser fetch API, but the ideas carry over to other stacks.

Your server is not a pipe.

Here’s the flow we’re building:

Browser ──POST /chat──► Your API ──stream──► LLM
Browser ◄───events───── Your API ◄──tokens── LLM

The thing that took me a while to internalize: your server is not a pipe. It sits in the middle of two connections, and either one can misbehave.

Something in front of it can buffer. The client behind it can leave. The provider underneath it can fail.

Most streaming bugs are one of these four hops going wrong.

For text chat, stream over fetch, not EventSource

You have three realistic options:

  • SSE via EventSource is good for simple server-to-browser streams. The catch: GET only, no custom headers, and it auto-reconnects by itself.
  • A streamed response via fetch is good for chat: POST body, auth headers, and abort support. The catch: you parse the stream yourself.
  • WebSocket is good for true two-way, low-latency traffic such as voice or live collaboration. The catch: more infrastructure, and it’s harder to scale and debug.

For a text chat UI, I’d go with fetch plus a streamed response. A chat request needs a message history and an auth token and EventSource can only do GET without custom headers.

EventSource also reconnects automatically when the connection drops. That sounds helpful, but for LLMs it can mean a second paid generation for the same question that nobody planned for. If you use it, make retries something you decide.

I’d reach for WebSockets when audio or real two-way traffic is involved. I’ve used one for a real-time voice assistant, and it’s the right tool there. For plain text answers, it adds complexity you don’t need.

Your proxy is holding the tokens.

This is the most common “works locally, not in prod” cause.

Reverse proxies like Nginx collect the upstream response and send it in bigger chunks by default. That’s great for normal pages and terrible for a stream. Your tokens sit in a buffer, and the user sees nothing until it fills or the response ends.

I’ve seen this called out as the most frequent production surprise with streaming, and it matches what the infrastructure docs say. Here’s what to check, in layers.

In your app, send headers that tell proxies to back off:

res.writeHead(200, {
  "Content-Type": "text/event-stream",
  "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
  "Connection": "keep-alive",
  "X-Accel-Buffering": "no", // Nginx-specific: don't buffer this response
});

In Nginx, for the streaming route:

location /api/chat {
    proxy_pass http://app;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    proxy_buffering off;      # the important one
    gzip off;                 # compression can re-buffer the stream
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;  # longer than your slowest answer
}

Anything else in front of you (CDN, load balancer, API gateway) may have its own buffering and idle timeout settings. I can’t tell you the right config for each one, and they change over time, so check your provider’s docs. What works everywhere is a test:

curl -N -X POST https://your-domain.com/api/chat \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"message":"count slowly from 1 to 20"}'

-N turns off curl's own buffering. If lines appear gradually, the whole path streams. If they arrive in one lump, something is buffering.

Run it against the real production URL, not just localhost, and again after any infrastructure change.

A closed tab has to cancel the LLM call.

This is the part I think is most underrated.

A user asks a question, sees it start answering, and closes the tab. What does your server do?

In a lot of apps, the honest answer is "nothing." The loop reading from the LLM keeps going, the provider keeps generating, and you pay for output nobody sees. Add a “Stop” button that only hides text in the UI, and you have the same problem with a friendlier face.

A real cancel has to travel the whole chain:

Browser:

const controller = new AbortController();
const res = await fetch("/api/chat", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ messages }),
  signal: controller.signal,
});
// Stop button:
stopButton.onclick = () => controller.abort();

Server:

app.post("/api/chat", async (req, res) => {
  const upstream = new AbortController();
  // If the client leaves before we finish, cancel the LLM call.
  res.on("close", () => {
    if (!res.writableEnded) upstream.abort();
  });
  res.writeHead(200, { "Content-Type": "text/event-stream" /* + headers above */ });
  try {
    const stream = await llm.chat.completions.create(
      { model, messages: req.body.messages, stream: true },
      { signal: upstream.signal }
    );
    for await (const chunk of stream) {
      const text = chunk.choices[0]?.delta?.content;
      if (text) res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify({ text })}

`);
    }
    res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify({ done: true })}

`);
  } catch (err) {
    if (!upstream.signal.aborted) {
      res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify({ error: "generation_failed" })}

`);
    }
  } finally {
    res.end();
  }
});

Some notes on choices I’d make again:

  • Listen to the response’s close event and check writableEnded. That separates "the client left early" from "we finished normally." In recent Node versions, I wouldn't rely on the request's close event for this.
  • Pass the same signal to everything the request started. If the question also triggered a vector search, a reranker, or tool calls, they should stop too. Otherwise you cancel the visible part and keep paying for the invisible part.
  • Don’t assume the provider stops billing immediately. Aborting the connection usually stops generation, but behavior varies by provider. I’d test it with a short script and check the usage numbers instead of trusting the docs alone.
  • Decide what to do with partial answers. If a user stops mid-answer, do you save what was generated? Choose on purpose.

The same idea shows up in voice. In a realtime voice assistant, “the user interrupted” is just cancellation with a microphone: the moment someone starts talking over the bot, you stop the bot’s audio and stop the work behind it.

After 200 OK, errors travel inside the stream.

Normally errors are status codes: 400, 429, 500. But in a stream, you’ve already sent 200 OK and some tokens before the problem happens. The provider times out, you hit a rate limit, or a tool call throws. The status code is already gone.

So errors have to travel inside the stream as events. Two rules I follow:

  1. Send an explicit error event so the UI can say something useful.
  2. Always send a final done event on success.

The second one is easy to skip, and it matters. Without done, the client can't tell "complete" from "the connection dropped after the third sentence." Users will read the truncated answer as the real answer.

In the UI I treat these as three separate end states:

  • Complete: got done
  • Failed: got error
  • Interrupted: the stream ended without either (show “response was cut off, try again”)

I’d also avoid silently auto-retrying a half-finished generation. A retry costs a second generation, and it might give a different answer from the one the user already half-read.

Network chunks are not events.

The client code looks simple. Two bugs got me.

Bug 1: network chunks don’t line up with your events. One read can contain half an event, or three and a half. If you parse each chunk directly, you’ll eventually hit a JSON.parse error on a partial line.

Keep a buffer, split on the blank line that ends each event, and carry the leftover:

const reader = res.body.getReader();
const decoder = new TextDecoder();
let buffer = "";
while (true) {
  const { value, done } = await reader.read();
  if (done) break;
  // stream: true keeps multi-byte characters intact across chunks
  buffer += decoder.decode(value, { stream: true });
  const events = buffer.split("

");
  buffer = events.pop(); // the last piece may be incomplete, keep it
  for (const evt of events) {
    if (!evt.startsWith("data: ")) continue; // skips heartbeat comments
    handle(JSON.parse(evt.slice(6)));
  }
}

Bug 2: broken characters. An emoji or a non-English character can be several bytes, and a chunk can end in the middle of one. Decoding each chunk separately gives you �.

The { stream: true } option on TextDecoder fixes it. This one is nasty because it passes every English-only test.

Render once per frame, not once per token

Tokens can arrive fast. If you re-render the whole message on every token, especially if you re-parse Markdown each time, the page starts to stutter.

What helps:

  • Batch updates. Collect incoming text and update the screen once per animation frame, not once per token.
  • Treat the streaming message as append-only, and avoid rebuilding earlier content.
  • Plan for half-finished Markdown. A code fence that hasn’t closed yet can make a renderer flicker.
  • Respect the user’s scroll. If they scrolled up to read, don’t pull them back down on every token.

And measure the right thing. Users will wait through a long answer if the first token arrives quickly. The time to the first token is worth logging more than the total duration.

A quiet connection gets cut.

Model answers can go quiet: the model is thinking, or a tool call takes several seconds. Some proxies and load balancers see silence and decide the connection is dead.

Two fixes:

  • Raise timeouts above your slowest realistic answer, on every layer.
  • Send a heartbeat. In SSE, a line starting with : is a comment that clients ignore.
const heartbeat = setInterval(() => res.write(": ping

"), 15000);
res.on("close", () => clearInterval(heartbeat));

If your answer involves tools, also stream status events like {"status": "searching documents"}. Ten seconds of silence feels broken. Ten seconds with "Looking that up…" feels normal.

One more: deploys. A rolling restart can kill streams that are mid-answer. Give your servers a graceful shutdown period at least as long as your longest answer.

Some answers should not stream

Streaming is great for text people read. It isn’t always right:

  • Structured output (JSON, function arguments) is useless half-finished. Wait and validate the whole thing.
  • Server-to-server calls gain nothing from streaming.
  • Answers you need to check before showing (safety filters, “does this match the tool results?”) can’t be checked until they’re done. Streaming and validation pull in opposite directions, and you have to pick which matters more.

Three things I have not solved yet

Because I’d rather be honest than sound finished:

  • Resumable streams. If a user refreshes mid-answer, can they pick up where they left off? I’ve read about approaches that write chunks to something like Redis Streams so a reconnect can resume, but I haven’t built this myself yet.
  • Scaling beyond one server. Long-lived connections behave differently under load balancing and autoscaling, and I’m still learning where the limits are.
  • Backpressure. If the client reads slower than you write, buffers grow on your side. I know the concept, but I haven’t pushed it hard enough in practice to have strong opinions.

If you’ve solved any of these, I’d love to hear how.

Run these ten checks before you ship

  • Tested through the real production path with curl -N, not just localhost
  • proxy_buffering off, X-Accel-Buffering: no, and no compression on the stream route
  • Browser AbortController wired to the Stop button
  • Server aborts the upstream LLM call (and tools or searches) on client disconnect
  • Errors sent as stream events, plus a final done event on success
  • UI shows three end states: complete, failed, interrupted
  • Client buffers partial events and decodes with stream: true
  • Rendering batched, and scroll behavior respects the user
  • Timeouts raised on every layer, with a heartbeat during quiet periods
  • Time to first token is logged

Getting tokens on screen is 10% of the work

The rest is deciding what happens when something in the middle misbehaves: a proxy that buffers, a user who leaves, a provider that fails, a connection that goes quiet.

A stream is a long-lived relationship between three parties, and any of them can disappear. Write the code for the moment they do.

medium.titulo: REQ-F05: Designing the Parking Issue Reporter
medium.resumo: By Torres, Sean Gabrielle | Section: IT3R4
medium.conteudo_html:
By Torres, Sean Gabrielle | Section: IT3R4

Picking My Requirement

Before selecting my requirement, I reviewed our group’s project pipeline to find a functional requirement that had not yet been designed in Part 3 or Part 4. While our group focused heavily on student-facing features, such as checking parking space availability (REQ-F01) and reading lot guidelines (REQ-F03)—REQ-F05 remained completely uncovered with no sequence diagram or wireframe.

REQ-F05 states: “The system shall display reported parking issues to authorized personnel.” It remained uncovered because our initial group design sprint prioritized the student rider’s immediate navigation experience rather than administrative workflows. However, during our user interviews, respondents explicitly complained about improperly parked bikes blocking exits and locked handlebars creating jams. Designing this feature ensures that student feedback actually reaches campus security to resolve physical lot jams.

Context Analysis

Meet Kuya Cardo, a campus security guard assigned to oversee the main motorcycle parking lot. It is 2:00 PM on a humid Tuesday — peak hours on campus — and the lot is crowded. While conducting his rounds on foot, students are continuously arriving and trying to maneuver past improperly parked motorcycles blocking exit routes.

Kuya Cardo doesn’t have time to sit at a desktop computer in an office, nor can he approach through unfiltered student complaints. He needs a mobile, real-time dashboard that instantly highlights severe physical obstructions so he can walk directly to the problematic spot, clear the pathway, or contact the owner before a complete traffic jam occurs.

Defining Requirements

  • Original REQ-ID: REQ-F05 — "The system shall display reported parking issues to authorized personnel."
  • Restated: When a student submits a report about a blocked pathway, improper parking, or a hazardous condition, the system must immediately present this flag on an administrative mobile screen for campus security, sorted by urgency and location.

Design

Design Annotations & Key Features:

  • Urgency-Based Badge & Color Coding: High-priority incidents (like blocked exit paths) appear at the top with prominent warning icons so guards can prioritize critical jams immediately.
  • Location Tag & Photo Thumbnail: Clearly states the exact zone and includes photo verification uploaded by the student so security staff can locate the issue without guessing.
  • One-Tap Action Buttons (“Resolve & Clear”): Allows guards to update issue status directly from their phones while standing in the parking lot.

Testing and Quality Assurance

Once the design was done, the next part was how I’d actually know it worked once it was built. Rather than a vague plan to “test it thoroughly,” I wrote this as if preparing a production-ready engineering spec, framing it as a specific test case with an ID, the exact steps to reproduce it, and a clear pass/fail line, so anyone on the team or me, could rerun it without guessing what “working” even means.

Quality Assurance Measures

  • Code Review: Before deployment, another team member reviews the issue-dispatching logic and API endpoint security to ensure unauthorized users cannot access the guard feed.
  • Regression Testing: TC-F05–01 is stored in the automated test suite to ensure future UI or database updates do not disrupt issue delivery.
  • Edge Case Check: Tests are performed with poor cellular connectivity in the parking lot to verify that issue reports queue locally and sync as soon as signal strength recovers.

Design Rationale

REQ-F05 is directly supported by this administrative issue dashboard, which turns student-submitted reports into actionable tasks for campus security. As highlighted in the context analysis, security guards like Kuya Cardo are constantly mobile and need immediate, clear details (such as photos and zone labels) without navigating complex menus. The one-tap action buttons and high-urgency sorting ensure that critical lot blockages are cleared rapidly.

A key limitation of this design is that it relies on active cellular or Wi-Fi data coverage across the entire campus lot. If a guard enters a signal dead zone, live updates may be delayed, requiring an offline synchronization fallback in future iterations.

medium.resumo: Was hinter SKILL.md steckt, warum inzwischen fast alle KI-Werkzeuge das Format verstehen und wie du deinen ersten Skill baust
medium.conteudo_html:
Was hinter SKILL.md steckt, warum inzwischen fast alle KI-Werkzeuge das Format verstehen und wie du deinen ersten Skill baust

Kennst du das?

Transparenzhinweis gemäß EU AI Act: Dieser Beitrag wurde mit Unterstützung eines KI-Schreibprogramms erstellt und von mir redaktionell geprüft. Auch die Grafiken sind mit KI-Unterstützung entstanden.

Du erklärst ChatGPT oder Claude zum zehnten Mal, wie dein Angebot aufgebaut ist. Welche Tonalität du willst. Welche Wörter tabu sind. Welches Format am Ende rauskommen soll. Am nächsten Tag fängst du wieder von vorne an.

Genau dieses Problem lösen Skills.

Ein Skill ist im Kern ein Ordner mit einer einzigen Pflichtdatei: der SKILL.md. Darin steht in normalem Text, wie eine bestimmte Aufgabe erledigt werden soll. Kein Programmieren, keine Schnittstelle, kein Entwickler nötig. Du schreibst dein Wissen einmal auf, und die KI holt es sich jedes Mal, wenn die Aufgabe ansteht.

Wie ein Skill aufgebaut ist

Eine SKILL.md hat zwei Teile.

Oben steht ein kurzer Kopfbereich mit zwei Angaben: einem Namen und einer Beschreibung. Die Beschreibung ist wichtiger, als sie aussieht. Sie sagt der KI, wann dieser Skill gebraucht wird.

Darunter folgen die eigentlichen Anweisungen. Schritt für Schritt, so wie du sie einem neuen Mitarbeiter erklären würdest. Wer mag, legt in denselben Ordner noch Vorlagen, Beispieltexte oder kleine Skripte dazu.

Das war’s. Eine Markdown-Datei. Ein Ordner.

Warum diese eine Datei so viel verändert, habe ich auch hier beschrieben: SKILL.md erklärt: Warum eine einzige Datei deine KI-Nutzung komplett verändert.

Der Trick dahinter: Die KI liest nur, was sie gerade braucht

Jetzt wird es spannend. Du kannst Dutzende Skills anlegen, ohne dass die KI langsamer oder unschärfer wird.

Das Prinzip heißt „Progressive Disclosure“ und läuft in drei Stufen ab (agentskills.io):

  1. Beim Start kennt die KI nur Name und Beschreibung jedes Skills.
  2. Passt eine Aufgabe zur Beschreibung, lädt sie die kompletten Anweisungen.
  3. Erst beim Ausführen greift sie bei Bedarf auf Vorlagen oder Skripte im Ordner zu.

Stell dir eine gut sortierte Werkstatt vor. Du hast nicht jedes Werkzeug gleichzeitig in der Hand. Du weißt, wo es hängt, und greifst zu, wenn du es brauchst.

Warum das Thema gerade so groß wird

Entwickelt hat das Format Anthropic, das Unternehmen hinter Claude. Ende 2025 wurde es als offener Standard veröffentlicht, und seitdem haben ihn sehr viele Werkzeuge übernommen.

Auf der offiziellen Seite agentskills.io stehen inzwischen unter anderem Claude, ChatGPT und Codex, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Cursor und die Gemini CLI. Dazu kommen Dutzende kleinere Agenten-Werkzeuge.

Das heißt für dich: Ein Skill, den du heute schreibst, ist nicht an ein einziges Programm gebunden. Du baust ihn einmal und nimmst ihn mit, wenn du das Werkzeug wechselst.

Kein Anbieter-Käfig. Dein Wissen bleibt deins.

Drei Beispiele aus dem Alltag

Ein Skill lohnt sich überall dort, wo du dieselbe Aufgabe immer wieder nach denselben Regeln erledigst.

Der Schreibstil-Skill. Du hältst fest, wie du schreibst: Du-Ansprache, kurze Sätze, bestimmte Wörter, die nie vorkommen dürfen. Jeder Text, den die KI für dich entwirft, klingt danach nach dir.

Der Angebots-Skill. Leistungen, Preislogik, Aufbau, Pflichtangaben. Die KI erstellt Angebote nach deinem Schema, statt jedes Mal ein neues zu erfinden.

Der Prüf-Skill. Eine Checkliste, die vor jeder Veröffentlichung abgearbeitet wird. Rechtschreibung, Quellen, Formatierung, Kennzeichnungspflichten.

Ich arbeite selbst mit solchen Skills für meine Buchproduktion. Wenn mir ein Fehler auffällt, wandert die Korrektur als neue Regel in den Skill. Der Fehler taucht danach nicht mehr auf.

Genau das ist der Unterschied zu einem Prompt. Ein Prompt ist weg, wenn der Chat endet. Ein Skill lernt mit dir mit.

Worauf du achten solltest

Skills können Skripte enthalten, die auf deinem Rechner ausgeführt werden. Installiere deshalb nur Skills aus Quellen, denen du vertraust, und lies die SKILL.md vorher durch. Sie ist schließlich nur Text.

Halte jeden Skill auf eine Aufgabe fokussiert. Ein Skill, der „alles rund ums Marketing“ abdecken soll, wird unscharf. Drei kleine Skills schlagen einen großen.

Schreib die Beschreibung so konkret wie möglich. „Hilft bei Texten“ ist zu vage. „Schreibt LinkedIn-Posts in meinem Stil, mit Hook, drei Absätzen und Call-to-Action“ trifft.

Dein erster Skill in drei Schritten

  1. Such dir eine Aufgabe, die du mindestens einmal pro Woche erledigst.
  2. Schreib auf, wie du sie erledigst. Ehrlich und vollständig, inklusive der Dinge, die „doch klar sind“.
  3. Leg daraus eine SKILL.md mit Name, Beschreibung und Anweisungen an und teste sie drei-, viermal. Was nicht passt, besserst du direkt in der Datei nach.

Nach einer Woche merkst du den Unterschied.

Wenn du es Schritt für Schritt lernen willst

Alles Weitere, von der Sicherheit bis zu Geschäftsmodellen mit Skills, steht in meinem Buch „SKILL.md: Dein erster KI-Agent“:

👉 Hier findest du das Buch auf Amazon: https://www.amazon.de/dp/B0DJ99PPK1

Welche Aufgabe würdest du als Erstes in einen Skill packen? Schreib es mir in die Kommentare.

medium.titulo: Opus 5.5 Video Examples: 13 Picks and the Prompts Behind Them
medium.resumo: An Opus 5.5 video is an animation that Claude Opus 5.5 writes as code; a browser draws it one frame at a time, and the frames are saved as…
medium.conteudo_html:
An Opus 5.5 video is an animation that Claude Opus 5.5 writes as code; a browser draws it one frame at a time, and the frames are saved as an MP4. The strongest ones look like motion design: crisp type, precise color, interface mockups, charts, and transitions in which one shape becomes the next.

Among 475 public Opus 5.5 videos, about six in ten are motion graphics, four in five are 16:9 landscape, and the median length is 30 seconds. The thirteen picks below cover showreels, launch films, interface motion, social ads, explainers, and illustrated stories, each with its prompt.

What Makes an Opus 5.5 Video Different

Veo, Kling, and Seedance paint pixels. Opus 5.5 takes another route: it writes a self-contained HTML file in Canvas, SVG, CSS, GSAP, or Three.js, a headless browser renders that file frame by frame, and ffmpeg encodes the output (Hugging Face walkthrough, Claude Video index). Canvas is the clear favorite, appearing in 336 of the 475 videos, with SVG in 193 and Three.js in 141. Video goes unmentioned on the Opus 5.5 announcement page; creators worked out this use for themselves.

Treating video as code has three consequences worth knowing before reading the picks:

  • Type stays crisp and color stays exact. Letters are rendered as real text, so a hex value written into the prompt is the hex value that appears on screen.
  • Revisions cost little. Reworking a scene comes down to editing a few lines of code.
  • Photorealism stays out of reach. Deedy Das, whose launch film appears further down, said of technical explainers: “photorealistic video gen like Seedance is not very useful here” (post).
  • Left to its defaults, Opus 5.5 drifts toward centered text over a gradient with every element fading in, which is why so many early videos looked interchangeable (Rexan Wong’s breakdown). Strong Opus 5.5 videos share four traits, each one visible within a few seconds of playback:
  1. The pacing varies, with quick cuts set against moments that hold for a beat.
  2. The type has a hierarchy: one dominant line, smaller supporting labels, an obvious reading order.
  3. The scenes are linked, with one shape carrying through into the next scene.
  4. The piece lands on a final card or a clean loop point.

Motion Design Showreels

1. The One-Sentence Showreel Prompt That Dozens of Creators Borrowed

The prompt fits on a single line:

make a dynamic 15-second motion graphics video that shows what an incredible motion designer you are, like it’s your showreel for a résumé. go all out.

Opus presented the result as a designer’s portfolio, complete with a timecode HUD and chapter labels. One chapter sets six easing curves running side by side beneath the line “Six ways to get from A to B.” Another floods the frame with a looping tile pattern. A single word slams in at poster scale before a red end card closes the reel. The prompt supplies a goal, a duration, and a level of ambition, then hands every creative choice to the model. That makes it a good test of the model, and a poor fit for anything tied to your own brand.

No fewer than 90 public Opus 5.5 videos reuse this sentence or something close to it, among them reels by Ajith (4,057 likes) and Leon Abboud, each with a different look. We gave Opus 5.5 the same sentence too:

Stephan’s version leaned on easing curves and tiles. Ours opens on a bouncing ball that bursts into the word “MOTION,” then travels through a wave of 2,304 dots and a ring of points that morphs from circle to square to star.

Product Launch Videos

Where the showreel gives the model total freedom, the next three picks put it to work for a product, each with a different amount of real information to go on.

2. A Startup Launch Film Spun From a Single Sentence

Deedy Das gave Opus almost nothing to work with. The full brief:

make a modern slick and punchy video for a modern startup that works on inference

With no company named, Opus made one up and called it “muda” (Japanese for waste). The film opens on a user waiting 2.81 seconds for an answer, cuts to a GPU cluster climbing to 94% utilization, and closes on a logo, with each scene tagged by a small numbered label in the manner of keynote chapters. Nobody asked for the sequence of problem, product, proof, and name; it arrived on its own. The whole piece took Deedy about a minute and roughly $2.

The product, the figures, and the name are all invented. A real launch needs those details to come from whoever writes the prompt.

3. A SaaS Launch That Borrows a Real Product’s Assets

Moritz Kremb went the other way, asking Opus to choose a recognizable product and fetch genuine assets for it:

I want you to create a highly professional SaaS product launch video. Go and find some SaaS, preferably just one that people know, so it’s easier to identify with it. Pick that, and then make sure to get actual assets and images and all of that stuff from the internet.

Opus settled on Notion and followed the standard launch-film cadence: “Docs here. Chats there. Tasks everywhere.” over drifting app icons, then a rebuilt project board, a feature line paired with a chart, a strip of customer logos, and finally an end card on which a cursor clicks through the call to action. The real product context is what gives the piece its specificity. Adapting it for your own product means pasting in screenshots, your headline, and your feature list. The brand and logos belong to Notion, so treat the clip as a demo.

4. A Photo-Print App Launch in One Unbroken Take

The launch from zero has the most detailed brief of the three: a prompt of several thousand characters spread across <inputs>, <direction>, <structure>, <build>, <gotchas>, and <start> blocks. The direction block begins:

An Apple-keynote launch film, 2D only, one continuous take. Every scene is made out of the previous one: nothing fades, blurs or cuts. […] Banned: crossfades, blur-ins, brightness “developing”, 3D flips, particles, glows, holds longer than 1s, anything that looks like a template.

On screen, a button turns into a photo, a glass slider relights it to golden hour, the image travels from a phone into a browser window, and the film finishes on a framed print hanging on real footage of a wall. Spelling out what is banned strips away the template look faster than piling on adjectives does. Before any of the film is written, the prompt makes Opus lay out a beat map and four still frames. The creator provided the photos, the soundtrack, and the wall footage, and the prompt asks for all three at the very start.

All three launch pieces share one arc: hook, product, a handful of features, end card. opus6.video packages that arc as its App launch video template, with a headline, three features, and a closing URL waiting for your own details.

UI Animation and App Walkthroughs

Next comes interface motion, and the second most-liked of the thirteen picks.

5. A Single Shape Morphing Through Nine Interface States

Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, never cut: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur. A cursor drives every change with real clicks and drags.

A lone black element becomes, in turn, a button, a checkmark, a music player, a volume slider, a toggle, a set of tabs, a chart, a ⌘K command palette, and a toast, before returning to the button. A cursor sets off each change in sync with a 120 BPM track, and because the last frame matches the first, the clip loops without a visible seam.

Two decisions carry the piece. Keeping one continuous object on screen sustains attention across fourteen seconds, and the prompt pins the tempo (“120 BPM, 7 bars, something happens on every beat”), which gives every morph a beat to land on. The states themselves are generic, so a version for a real app would swap in real screens. opus6.video’s Product walkthrough template is designed for that variant: a cursor clicking its way through your interface.

Social Ads and Brand Bumpers

6. A Vertical Fintech Ad Built for the Phone

make a punchy and modern short video for social that promotes @lightspark capabilities. Needs to be production grade with sound

Each screen carries a single idea in large type on a light grid: “Money still moves like it’s 1973,” a USD-to-MXN transfer completing “In seconds,” then “For humans. And AI agents” and “The TCP/IP of money” before the logo appears. The pitch rests on the gap between a 1973 date and an instant transfer, and every line stays legible on a phone with the sound off.

7. A 20-Second Kinetic Identity Bumper

TechHalla wrote the prompt as a spec sheet:

DURATION: exactly 20.00 seconds. LOOPABLE: frame 0 == frame last (position, opacity, cursor if any).
FORMAT: one HTML file, 1080×1080 (square, X-native). 60fps.
PALETTE (strict): bg #0A0A0A, magenta #FF2BD6, acid green #B8FF00 […] No other hue

The result is heavy white type on black, scrambled acid-green characters settling into words, and a handle that types itself out across a magenta bar. All of it comes from numbers: a precise 20.00-second loop, 60fps, and three hex codes paired with “no other hue.” The palette can be swapped for your own as long as the precision stays. With so little room for content, a bumper like this does its best work as an intro or outro.

For short branded work, opus6.video supports 9:16 and 1:1 formats and includes a Logo reveal template. Its effect library catalogs motion styles like the ones above (letter drop, decode scramble, stretch slide-in), each with exact wording ready to paste into a prompt.

Explainers and Data Stories

8. A Negroni Recipe, Measured Out Step by Step

We’re going to try a little test. Do you think you could render a recipe motion graphic animation using javascript or html (w/e you think will produce the best) to show the full recipe from start to finish (empty glass to completed cocktail) — Explainer video style — Showing the recipe ingreidents + measurements as they’re going into the cup. Should be a 30s video.

Rory left the cocktail unnamed, and Opus picked a Negroni. A hand-drawn glass fills layer by layer, with measurement ticks running up its side. A step card reads “1 oz GIN” or “20 SEC STIR,” while a six-step progress bar at the foot of the frame ticks off ice, gin, Campari, vermouth, stir, and peel in real time.

The tracker is the detail most worth taking. Any step-by-step video becomes easier to follow once viewers can see where they are in the sequence. When a particular recipe or product matters, name it in the prompt, or the model will choose one on your behalf.

9. Recursion, Taught in a New Style Every Scene

A video explaining recursion, where every explanation about recursion has a radically different video style, make this self-referential & clever & fast moving.

Ethan Mollick’s video teaches recursion by being recursive. Each explanation sits inside the previous one and jumps genre: corporate explainer, nature documentary, movie trailer, kids’ TV. A “call stack” bar along the top grows deeper with every layer, and the video ends by playing inside itself beneath “STILL CONFUSED?”

10. Milestones From the History of AI

klöss wrote the shortest prompt in the explainer group:

make a video highlighting key moments in the history of AI.

From that line, Opus produced a dark, orange-accented timeline split into numbered chapters: the artificial neuron of 1943 rendered as a logic diagram, a 1966 ELIZA exchange typed out on a terminal, a bar chart of the 2012 ImageNet results. Narration runs as captions along the lower edge, and the final card lists Claude as the author of the motion design, the sound design, and the code. Timelines play to the strengths of code animation, since every moment on one is a line of text, a number, or a simple diagram.

Every date and figure in the piece came from Opus alone, so an explainer like this needs a fact-check before it goes out.

Text, numbers, and diagrams are the raw material of all three explainers, and that is where code animation is strongest. opus6.video offers Explainer, Data story, and Recipe & how-to templates for this format. Its cap of 30 seconds per video means a longer explainer in the vein of #9 or #10 would need to be broken into parts.

Story and History Animations

11. The Human Story as an Origami Doodle

Create a short origami / doodle-style animation showing humanity’s development, progress, and civilization from birth to the present, and ultimately the hatching of AI. […] Style: doodly, cute, warm, strongly narrative, no spoken language (simple text is OK, but don’t use too much explanatory/narrative text, because I want different civilizations to be able to understand it), poetic, moving, high quality.

The story begins on soft paper-cut hills at dawn and a first settlement, moves on to the Earth at night strung with glowing icons, network lines spreading across a village, and a closing sketchbook page where a pencil draws a small creature. The request for “no spoken language” pushed the entire story into images, so the piece plays in any market without translation.

12. 250 Years of U.S. History, Told in Sand

Make a 2-minute sand animation that tells the story of 250 years of U.S. history. Keep it lively, engaging, and tasteful. Add appropriate background music and sound design.

Each scene is built from grainy sepia silhouettes and stamped with a year in the corner: wagons rolling west in the 1840s, the Statue of Liberty greeting a passing steamship in 1886 beneath the line “Give me your tired, your poor…”, crowds gathering in 1963, and finally fireworks above “250, 1776–2026.” The two words “sand animation” were enough to bring sepia grain, silhouettes, and scene changes that look like sand being swept aside.

13. Four Seasons Through a Train Window

4 seasons passing outside a train window, a cozy carriage, a cup of coffee on the table, Grand Budapest Hotel style

The frame never moves. Purple curtains, two table lamps, and a coffee cup hold their symmetrical places as the view cycles from spring to summer, autumn, and winter, then returns to blossom, a pink palace perched on a far hill throughout. Naming the film supplied the symmetry, the pastel palette, and the pink building in four words.

All three story prompts name a medium or a reference: origami, sand, a Wes Anderson film.

What These Examples Have in Common

The one-line showreel prompt yielded polished reels that could belong to anyone, while the launch films that pass for a real company were fed real context: a product, screenshots, a palette, supplied photos or footage. Rexan Wong summed it up this way: “everyone has the same model. the context you give it is what makes it look pro” (post, 6,730 likes).

Six of the 13 prompts set a duration or tempo, and they include the two most-liked picks (#1 and #5). Across all 475 public videos, half run between 15 and 43 seconds. When the prompt leaves length open, Opus decides for itself: klöss’s one-line history prompt specified no length and returned a film of nearly three minutes.

Several prompts also name a style: origami, sand animation, Grand Budapest Hotel, Apple keynote, Dribbble-level UI motion. Every one of those references carries a palette and a pace that would otherwise take a full paragraph to describe.

The longest prompts plan before they animate. They request a beat map, a state list, or still frames ahead of any code, so problems surface while fixing them is still cheap.

Effort ranges widely. The quickest piece took about a minute and $2 (Deedy Das); the slowest, a launch video whose soundtrack was itself written in code, took about eight hours (Leon Lin). Between those two sit 15 minutes (Chain), 19 minutes with two revisions (David Ch), and three prompts (Miles).

What Opus 5.5 Videos Can’t Do

  • It cannot film anything. A realistic person or place calls for a video generation model such as Veo or Seedance, or for a camera. Opus can then cut that footage and layer type and graphics over it, provided the environment can read your video files. Claude Code paired with Remotion is one such environment: its <OffthreadVideo> component drops video clips into a composition. opus6.video builds videos from a description and does not accept video input.
  • It will not record a real song or voiceover. The music in #4 and #5 was supplied by the creators, with Opus syncing the animation to it. Audio written as code is possible too, and Leon Lin used it for an entire soundtrack plus sound effects, yet any recorded song or voiceover has to be brought in from outside.
  • It has no knowledge of your brand. Without a reference, a logo, and a palette, the output slides back toward the same centered-text look.

Make Your Own Opus 5.5 Video

The right starting point depends on what is already in hand:

  • To gauge what the model can do, run the showreel prompt from #1.
  • To announce a product, borrow the launch structure of examples #2 through #4 and fill it with your product name, three features, and brand colors.
  • For anything longer than 30 seconds, or to bring in your own footage and audio, work in Claude Code with a renderer such as Remotion or HyperFrames.

Build the Pipeline Yourself

Pair Claude Code with a render pipeline that opens the HTML in a headless browser, captures every frame, and encodes the result with ffmpeg. The Hugging Face walkthrough covers the specifics. This path supports long videos, audio, and footage.

Work in a Browser Tool

opus6.video runs Claude Opus 5.5 on your behalf, so you need neither a Claude subscription nor a local setup. Describe the video, or begin from a template such as Designer showreel, App launch video, or Product walkthrough, then set the format to 16:9, 9:16, or 1:1 and the length to 10, 15, or 30 seconds. Opus 5.5 drafts a storyboard and then the scenes; you refine them in chat and download a 1080p MP4. Exported videos are silent, so add music in your editor.

More finished videos, each shown with its prompt, are collected in the opus6.video examples gallery.

FAQ

How Long Can an Opus 5.5 Video Run?

When you render it yourself, there is no fixed ceiling; the picks above range from 14 seconds to almost 3 minutes. Longer videos take longer to render, because every frame is drawn and captured one at a time. On opus6.video, each video runs up to 30 seconds.

Can These Prompts Be Reused?

Yes, as a starting point. Replace the product, subject, and palette with your own. The videos themselves belong to their creators, so link to the original posts when you reference them.

medium.conteudo_html:
SaaS Laravel: Stop Rebuilding the Same SaaS Features Every Time. Starting a new SaaS product is exciting.

You have an idea, you know what you want to build, and you want to start working on the part that actually makes your product different.

Then reality hits.

Before you can work on the real product, you end up building the same things again:

  • Authentication
  • User profiles
  • Teams
  • Permissions
  • Invitations
  • Notifications
  • Settings
  • Activity logs
  • Dashboard layouts
  • Account management
  • Frontend components
  • Error states
  • Email flows

None of these features are unusual.

But almost every SaaS application needs them.

And rebuilding them for every new project takes a lot of time.

That is why I built SaaS Laravel.

Website: https://saas-laravel.com/

What Is SaaS Laravel?

SaaS Laravel is a set of Laravel starter kits built for developers who want a solid starting point for a SaaS application.

The idea is simple:

Start with the common SaaS work already organized, then spend your time building your actual product.

It is not a no-code platform.

It is not a closed system.

And it is not trying to hide Laravel from you.

You still work with your Laravel application normally. You own the code, you can change it, extend it, remove parts you do not need, or build completely new features on top of it.

SaaS Laravel simply gives you a better place to start.

Why I Built It

Whenever I started a new SaaS project, I noticed the same pattern.

I would spend the first few days or weeks rebuilding things I had already built before.

Create authentication.

Create the dashboard.

Add user settings.

Add team members.

Create invitations.

Add permissions.

Create notifications.

Build common frontend components.

Handle empty states.

Add profile pages.

Set up project structure.

And only after all of that could I start working on the feature that actually made the product interesting.

That felt wasteful.

So instead of rebuilding the same foundation for every project, I wanted one clean base that I could reuse.

That became SaaS Laravel.

Start With the Essentials Already in Place

A starter kit should save time without making the code difficult to understand.

That is why SaaS Laravel focuses on features that most SaaS products need sooner or later.

You start with a working foundation and then shape it around your product.

Some of the common pieces include:

  • Authentication
  • User accounts
  • Teams
  • Member management
  • Permissions
  • Invitations
  • Notifications
  • Settings
  • Activity-related features
  • Reusable UI
  • Common layouts
  • Developer-friendly project structure

Instead of starting from an empty project, you start from something that already feels like an application.

Authentication Is Already Part of the Foundation

Authentication is usually one of the first things we build.

Login.

Registration.

Password reset.

Email verification.

Account-related pages.

It is necessary, but it is rarely the reason someone is building a SaaS product.

SaaS Laravel gives you a working authenticated application so you can move on to more important product work.

You can still customize the flow whenever your application needs something different.

Teams Without Building Everything From Scratch

A lot of SaaS products eventually become multi-user products.

One person creates an account.

Then they want to invite a teammate.

Then another.

Soon you need:

  • Team members
  • Invitations
  • Access control
  • Member management
  • Different permissions

This can quickly become a project of its own.

SaaS Laravel gives this part a clear structure from the beginning.

Instead of figuring out the entire team system while building your actual product, you already have a foundation you can extend.

Simple Permission Management

Not every user should be able to do everything.

An owner may have full access.

Another user may only be able to view data.

Someone else may be able to create records but not delete them.

These rules become important very quickly in real SaaS products.

SaaS Laravel includes a straightforward permission approach so your application can control access without turning permission management into unnecessary complexity.

The important part is that you can adapt it to your own product rules.

Invitations That Feel Like Part of the Product

Inviting someone sounds like a small feature.

But once you build it properly, you need to think about:

  • Who can invite users?
  • What happens if the email is already registered?
  • What happens if it is not?
  • When does an invitation expire?
  • Can it be resent?
  • Can it be cancelled?
  • What access should the invited person receive?

These are small decisions individually, but together they take time.

A starter kit should give you a sensible starting point instead of making you solve the same problem again.

Notifications Without Reinventing the UI

Notifications appear in almost every modern application.

A team member joins.

Something is updated.

A task completes.

An invitation arrives.

An important action needs the user’s attention.

Creating the backend event is only one part of the job.

You also need a usable interface for displaying notifications and handling read/unread states.

SaaS Laravel provides a foundation for this so notifications can feel like a normal part of your application instead of another standalone feature you need to design from zero.

Settings Should Be Easy to Extend

Every application eventually grows a settings area.

At first, maybe it is only the user’s name and email.

Later you may need:

  • Account settings
  • Team settings
  • Application preferences
  • Notification preferences
  • Security settings
  • Product-specific configuration

SaaS Laravel gives settings a clear home in the application.

You can keep adding your own options without turning the settings area into an unorganized collection of pages.

A UI You Can Actually Change

A starter kit should not force you to keep its design forever.

Your product will have its own brand.

Its own colors.

Its own layout decisions.

Its own components.

That is expected.

The purpose of the included UI is to save you from beginning with a blank page.

Use it as it is when it works for you.

Change it when it does not.

The code is yours.

Choose Your Frontend

Different developers prefer different frontend frameworks.

Some prefer Vue.

Some work faster in React.

Others enjoy Svelte.

SaaS Laravel is designed around that reality.

You can choose the frontend you are comfortable with instead of changing your entire development workflow just because a starter kit picked one framework.

The available starter-kit options include:

  • Vue
  • React
  • Svelte

The important part is that they share the same Laravel foundation.

One Laravel Foundation, Multiple Frontend Choices

Maintaining separate Laravel applications for Vue, React, and Svelte would create unnecessary duplication.

Fix something in one project and you would have to repeat the same change in the others.

That is exactly what I wanted to avoid.

The goal of SaaS Laravel is to keep the common backend foundation consistent while allowing different frontend implementations.

Conceptually:

Laravel
                │
        Shared SaaS Core
                │
      ┌─────────┼─────────┐
      │         │         │
     Vue      React     Svelte

The business foundation stays familiar.

You choose how you want to render the product.

Use It As-Is or Make It Yours

SaaS Laravel is not intended to be a rigid template.

Think of it as a starting point.

Maybe you need everything it provides.

Maybe you only need half of it.

That is fine.

You can:

  • Remove features
  • Rename things
  • Change layouts
  • Replace components
  • Add your own modules
  • Change the data model
  • Build your own business logic
  • Customize the frontend completely

A starter kit should make your first steps faster, not decide what your final product must look like.

Built for Real Development

A polished screenshot is nice.

But developers eventually have to work with the code.

That is why project structure matters.

When a project grows, you need to know where things belong.

You should be able to open the application a few months later and still understand how it is organized.

SaaS Laravel aims to keep the structure predictable so adding new features does not slowly turn the project into something difficult to maintain.

Common Components Save More Time Than You Think

Buttons, inputs, selects, checkboxes, labels and validation messages seem small.

But when every page creates its own version, inconsistency starts to appear quickly.

One button looks different.

Another input handles errors differently.

One page uses a different spacing system.

A reusable component layer helps keep those small details consistent.

That means when you improve one common component, many parts of the application improve with it.

Built With Customization in Mind

There is a big difference between a starter kit and a finished SaaS product.

Your product will still need its own:

  • Database design
  • Business rules
  • Workflows
  • Features
  • Branding
  • Integrations
  • Emails
  • Pricing
  • Product experience

And that is exactly where your development time should go.

The starter kit handles the common foundation.

You build the part people are actually paying for.

Developer Experience Matters

A good starter kit should reduce friction.

You should not spend hours trying to understand why something was built in an unusual way.

The code should feel familiar to someone already comfortable with Laravel.

That is also why I prefer keeping the product close to normal Laravel development rather than hiding everything behind proprietary abstractions.

You are still building a Laravel application.

You simply begin further ahead.

AI Coding Tools Work Better With Consistent Structure

AI coding assistants are becoming part of normal development workflows.

But they work much better when a project has clear patterns.

If one feature uses one folder structure and the next feature uses a completely different approach, generated code can quickly become inconsistent.

A predictable starter-kit structure gives both developers and coding agents a clearer pattern to follow.

For example, instead of asking an AI agent to invent an entire user-management architecture, you can ask it to extend the existing structure.

That usually produces cleaner results and requires less cleanup afterwards.

You Still Own the Code

This is important.

SaaS Laravel is meant to help developers build their own products.

It should not turn your application into something you cannot control.

You get the code.

You work with it directly.

You can understand it.

And you can change it.

There is no reason your SaaS product should become dependent on a visual builder or proprietary runtime just because you wanted to save some development time at the beginning.

Who Is SaaS Laravel For?

SaaS Laravel can be useful if you are:

  • Building your first SaaS
  • Launching another SaaS product
  • Creating an internal business tool
  • Building a client SaaS application
  • Prototyping a product
  • Creating a micro-SaaS
  • Working alone
  • Working with a small team

It is especially useful if you already know Laravel and want to spend less time rebuilding common application infrastructure.

Who Probably Does Not Need It?

Not every project needs a starter kit.

If you are building a very small application with only one or two pages, starting with a fresh Laravel installation may be perfectly fine.

And if your project has an extremely unusual architecture, you may prefer building everything yourself.

SaaS Laravel is most useful when your project looks like a typical modern SaaS application and you would otherwise spend time recreating the same common features.

The Goal Is Simple: Ship Faster

The goal is not to generate an entire SaaS business for you.

The goal is to remove unnecessary repetition.

Instead of this:

New idea
   ↓
Build authentication
   ↓
Build dashboard
   ↓
Build teams
   ↓
Build permissions
   ↓
Build invitations
   ↓
Build notifications
   ↓
Build settings
   ↓
Finally start the product

You can get closer to this:

New idea
   ↓
Start with SaaS Laravel
   ↓
Customize the foundation
   ↓
Build your actual product

That is the difference I wanted from a starter kit.

One-Time Access

I also wanted the purchasing model to stay simple.

Instead of another recurring development subscription, the starter kits are offered with one-time access.

Choose the framework you actually use, or get access to the complete set if you work across multiple frontend stacks.

The current options and details are available directly on the website.

View the starter kits:
https://saas-laravel.com/

Start With a Better Foundation

Building a SaaS product is already difficult.

There are plenty of real problems to solve:

Finding customers.

Building something useful.

Improving onboarding.

Listening to feedback.

Fixing bugs.

Shipping new features.

You probably do not need to add “build another settings screen from scratch” to that list.

That is what SaaS Laravel is for.

A clean starting point.

Common SaaS features already organized.

Laravel code you can actually work with.

And the freedom to turn it into your own product.

If you are starting a Laravel SaaS and want to spend more time on the product instead of rebuilding the foundation, take a look:

SaaS Laravel
