medium.conteudo_html:
Building a form in Laravel is easy.

Building dozens of forms while keeping validation, frontend fields, permissions, conditional logic, file uploads, and UI behavior consistent is where things start getting complicated.

In a typical Laravel + Inertia application, you may define validation rules in PHP, create the same fields again in Vue or React, handle errors on the frontend, add authorization rules somewhere else, and repeat the same setup for every new form.

After a while, a simple form becomes a collection of duplicated code spread across the backend and frontend.

That is exactly the problem Laravel Inertia Forms is built to solve.

Laravel Inertia Forms lets you define your form structure in PHP and render it in Vue, React, or Svelte through Inertia.

Instead of maintaining separate form definitions across your application, you get a single, predictable way to build forms.

GitHub: https://github.com/eramitgupta/laravel-Inertia-forms
Documentation: https://erag.in/laravel-inertia-forms/

Why I Built Laravel Inertia Forms

I build Laravel applications with Inertia regularly, and forms are one of those areas where the same code appears again and again.

Imagine a user form containing:

  • Name
  • Email
  • Phone
  • Country
  • Role
  • Profile image
  • Status
  • Permissions

On the Laravel side, you need validation and authorization.

On the frontend, you need to recreate the fields, labels, options, errors, disabled states, default values, and submission behavior.

Now imagine doing the same thing for customers, products, invoices, companies, settings, subscriptions, team members, and dozens of other resources.

The problem is not that forms are difficult.

The problem is repetition.

I wanted a form system where Laravel could describe the form once and the frontend could simply render it.

That idea became Laravel Inertia Forms.

What Is Laravel Inertia Forms?

Laravel Inertia Forms is a server-driven form builder for Laravel applications using Inertia.

The idea is simple:

PHP Form Definition
        ↓
      Inertia
        ↓
Frontend Renderer
        ↓
Vue / React / Svelte

Laravel defines the form.

The frontend renders it.

Your application still uses normal Laravel validation, authorization, models, controllers, and Inertia pages. The form builder simply provides a consistent contract between the backend and frontend.

This keeps form logic organized and reduces the amount of repetitive frontend code you need to maintain.

Define Forms in PHP

Instead of manually recreating every form field on the frontend, you can describe the form in PHP.

A simple form could conceptually look like this:

class UserForm
{
    public function fields(): array
    {
        return [
            Text::make('name')
                ->label('Name')
                ->required(),
            Email::make('email')
                ->label('Email')
                ->required(),
            Select::make('country')
                ->label('Country')
                ->options([
                    'in' => 'India',
                    'us' => 'United States',
                    'uk' => 'United Kingdom',
                ]),
        ];
    }
}

Your frontend receives the form definition and renders the appropriate components.

That means your form structure lives in one predictable place.

When you need to add a field, change a label, update a rule, or adjust the configuration, you don’t have to hunt through multiple frontend components.

One Form Definition, Multiple Frontends

One of the biggest goals of Laravel Inertia Forms is frontend flexibility.

The same form definition can be rendered with:

  • Vue
  • React
  • Svelte

This is especially useful if you maintain multiple products or starter kits.

For example, you might have:

Laravel Backend
     │
     ├── Vue Application
     ├── React Application
     └── Svelte Application

The UI implementation can be different for each framework, while the form contract remains consistent.

Instead of maintaining three completely separate form architectures, you can keep the form definition on the Laravel side and let each renderer handle its own presentation.

22+ Field Types

Real applications need more than text inputs.

Laravel Inertia Forms supports a broad collection of field types for common application requirements.

Depending on your form, you can work with fields such as:

  • Text
  • Email
  • Password
  • Number
  • Textarea
  • Select
  • Multi-select
  • Checkbox
  • Radio
  • Date
  • DateTime
  • File
  • Hidden
  • Toggle
  • Combobox
  • Searchable selections
  • Repeatable fields
  • Custom fields

This means you can build anything from a simple contact form to a large administration form without creating every control from scratch.

Laravel Validation Stays Where It Belongs

Laravel already provides one of the strongest validation systems in the PHP ecosystem.

There is no reason to replace it.

With Laravel Inertia Forms, your important validation rules can stay on the Laravel side.

For example:

Text::make('name')
    ->rules([
        'required',
        'string',
        'max:255',
    ]);
Email::make('email')
    ->rules([
        'required',
        'email',
    ]);

When validation fails, the frontend can display the errors returned by Laravel.

This helps avoid situations where your backend says one thing while your frontend validation says something different.

Your backend remains the source of truth.

Conditional Fields

Many real-world forms are dynamic.

Suppose you have this question:

Are you registering as a business?

If the user selects Yes, you may want to display:

  • Company name
  • Tax number
  • Company address
  • Registration number

If they select No, those fields should stay hidden.

This type of conditional behavior appears everywhere:

  • Checkout forms
  • Registration forms
  • SaaS onboarding
  • Customer forms
  • Job applications
  • Surveys
  • Product configuration
  • Administration panels

Laravel Inertia Forms supports conditional field behavior so you can keep these relationships organized as part of your form definition.

That is much cleaner than spreading conditional logic across several frontend components.

Multi-Step Forms

Some forms are simply too large for one screen.

A business onboarding form, for example, might include:

Step 1 — Personal Information

Name, email, phone number.

Step 2 — Company Details

Company name, registration number, industry.

Step 3 — Address

Street, city, state, country.

Step 4 — Preferences

Language, notifications, settings.

Step 5 — Review

Let the user review everything before submitting.

Breaking a large form into smaller steps creates a better experience and makes the form easier to understand.

Laravel Inertia Forms can support structured multi-step workflows without forcing you to build completely separate forms for every step.

Authorization

Not every field should be visible or editable by every user.

Consider an account management form.

A regular user may be allowed to edit:

  • Name
  • Email
  • Profile image

An administrator may additionally be allowed to edit:

  • Account status
  • Permissions
  • Internal notes
  • Administrative settings

Instead of relying only on frontend conditions, authorization can remain connected to your Laravel application.

That gives you a more predictable and secure architecture.

The frontend renders what the backend allows.

Model Binding

Most application forms eventually need to edit existing data.

You may be editing:

  • Users
  • Products
  • Customers
  • Orders
  • Companies
  • Invoices
  • Projects

Without a structured system, you often end up manually mapping model values into form data again and again.

Model binding helps reduce that work.

When editing an existing record, your form can work with the model’s current values and use them as the initial form state.

That makes create and edit forms much easier to maintain.

File Uploads

File uploads often introduce another layer of form complexity.

Applications may need users to upload:

  • Profile photos
  • Product images
  • Company logos
  • Documents
  • PDFs
  • Attachments
  • Certificates

Instead of creating a completely separate architecture for uploads, file fields can be handled as part of the same form system.

This keeps the developer experience consistent whether your form contains simple text fields or uploaded files.

Reusable Fieldsets

Large forms quickly become difficult to understand when every field is displayed in one long list.

A better approach is to organize related fields into sections.

For example:

Personal Information

  • First name
  • Last name
  • Email
  • Phone

Address

  • Address line
  • City
  • State
  • Postal code
  • Country

Company Information

  • Company name
  • Registration number
  • Tax number
  • Website

This structure improves both the user experience and the code organization.

Reusable field groups also make it easier to maintain forms that share common sections.

Searchable Comboboxes

A normal select field works well when you have five options.

It becomes painful when you have 5,000.

Imagine selecting a customer from thousands of records using a traditional dropdown.

That is not a good experience.

Searchable combobox fields are useful for selecting large datasets such as:

  • Customers
  • Suppliers
  • Products
  • Countries
  • Cities
  • Team members
  • Projects

Users can search instead of scrolling through a huge list.

For admin applications and SaaS dashboards, this can make a significant difference to usability.

Custom Fields

Every application is different.

Eventually, you will need a field that isn’t included in the default collection.

Maybe your project needs:

  • Rich text editor
  • Address autocomplete
  • Product selector
  • Color picker
  • Media manager
  • Permission selector
  • Tag selector
  • Date range picker
  • Custom search component

A good form builder should not lock you into its built-in fields.

Laravel Inertia Forms is designed to remain extensible, allowing application-specific components to participate in the same form system.

Accessible Forms

Developer experience matters, but user experience matters more.

Forms should work well for people using:

  • Keyboards
  • Screen readers
  • Different screen sizes
  • Different input methods

A reusable form system also creates an opportunity to standardize things such as:

  • Labels
  • Error messages
  • Focus states
  • Required field indicators
  • Keyboard interaction
  • Disabled states
  • Accessible markup

Instead of fixing accessibility separately across dozens of forms, improvements to your shared form components can benefit your entire application.

Consistent Forms Across Your Application

One issue I regularly see in large applications is that every developer builds forms differently.

One page has labels above fields.

Another has inline labels.

One component handles errors correctly.

Another does not.

One form uses a custom select.

Another uses a completely different implementation.

Over time, the application becomes inconsistent.

A structured form builder solves part of this problem.

Your form components can share the same:

  • Visual language
  • Error handling
  • Loading behavior
  • Disabled states
  • Field spacing
  • Labels
  • Validation feedback
  • Accessibility behavior

The result is not just cleaner code.

It is also a more consistent product.

Forms Without All the Wiring

A normal form often requires a surprising amount of wiring.

You create the fields.

Then the frontend state.

Then validation.

Then errors.

Then loading states.

Then conditional visibility.

Then permissions.

Then default values.

Then submission.

Then reset behavior.

Then edit-mode values.

Laravel Inertia Forms aims to reduce this repetitive setup by giving these pieces a common structure.

Instead of thinking about how every input should be connected, you can focus more on what the form actually needs to do.

AI-Friendly Form Development

AI coding tools are increasingly becoming part of everyday software development.

Structured form definitions work particularly well with these tools.

Imagine asking your coding agent:

Create a customer form with name, email, phone, company, country, account status, and an optional VAT number when the customer is a business.

Without an established form system, the AI may need to create or modify:

  • Laravel validation
  • Vue or React fields
  • Error handling
  • Conditional logic
  • Select options
  • Submit handling
  • Styling
  • Permissions

Every project might implement these things differently.

With Laravel Inertia Forms, the agent can work with an existing convention.

That makes generated code more predictable and easier to review.

The goal is not to make AI write everything.

The goal is to give both humans and AI agents a consistent structure to work with.

Build Once, Render Three Ways

Frontend frameworks change.

Some Laravel developers prefer Vue.

Some prefer React.

Others enjoy working with Svelte.

Your business requirements, however, usually remain the same.

A customer still needs:

  • Name
  • Email
  • Phone
  • Address

regardless of which frontend framework you selected.

That is why separating the form definition from its renderer makes sense.

Laravel
                │
                ▼
        PHP Form Definition
                │
          ┌─────┼─────┐
          ▼     ▼     ▼
         Vue  React  Svelte

Each frontend can use its own components and UI system while consuming the same form definition.

From PHP Class to Working Form

The overall workflow is intentionally simple.

1. Define the Form

Create your form definition in Laravel.

Configure fields, rules, options, authorization, conditions, and other behavior.

2. Pass It Through Inertia

The structured form data is made available to your Inertia page.

3. Render It

Your Vue, React, or Svelte renderer reads the form definition and creates the interface.

4. Submit Normally

The form still works with your Laravel application.

Validation, controllers, models, services, policies, and other Laravel features remain available.

You are not replacing Laravel.

You are reducing form boilerplate.

Where Can You Use Laravel Inertia Forms?

Laravel Inertia Forms is especially useful in applications containing a lot of structured data entry.

Examples include:

  • SaaS products
  • CRM systems
  • ERP applications
  • Admin dashboards
  • Internal company tools
  • E-commerce administration
  • Booking platforms
  • Customer portals
  • Project management tools
  • Content management systems
  • HR applications
  • Accounting applications
  • Inventory systems
  • Developer tools

The more forms your application has, the more useful a standardized form system becomes.

It Doesn’t Replace Inertia

Laravel Inertia Forms is not trying to replace Inertia.

It works with it.

You can continue using your existing:

  • Laravel controllers
  • Form requests
  • Validation rules
  • Policies
  • Eloquent models
  • Services
  • Inertia pages
  • Vue components
  • React components
  • Svelte components

The form builder simply creates a cleaner contract between Laravel and your frontend.

It Doesn’t Lock Your UI

Using a form builder should not mean losing control over your application’s design.

Your frontend renderer is still responsible for how the form looks and feels.

That means your application can maintain its own:

  • Design system
  • Components
  • Spacing
  • Typography
  • Themes
  • Responsive behavior
  • Dark mode
  • Accessibility standards

The PHP definition describes the form.

The frontend decides how that form should look.

This separation is important because business logic and presentation should not become unnecessarily coupled.

A Better Developer Experience for Large Applications

For a small project containing two forms, manually creating everything may be perfectly fine.

The benefits become much more noticeable as your application grows.

Imagine maintaining:

  • 10 forms
  • 30 forms
  • 50 forms
  • 100+ forms

At that scale, small inconsistencies and duplicated logic add up quickly.

A structured form system can help make forms:

  • Easier to create
  • Easier to review
  • Easier to maintain
  • Easier to reuse
  • Easier to test
  • Easier to extend
  • More consistent

The goal is not abstraction for the sake of abstraction.

The goal is to remove repetitive work that doesn’t provide additional value.

Open Source

Laravel Inertia Forms is open source.

You can inspect the source code, use it in your projects, report bugs, suggest improvements, or contribute to the project.

If you find the project useful, consider starring the repository. It helps other Laravel developers discover the package.

GitHub Repository

https://github.com/eramitgupta/laravel-Inertia-forms

Documentation

https://erag.in/laravel-inertia-forms/

The documentation contains the information you need to start using the package and explore its available form features.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Laravel Inertia Forms?

Laravel Inertia Forms is a form builder that lets you define your form structure in PHP and render it inside an Inertia application.

It is designed to reduce repetitive form code and create a consistent form architecture.

Does it replace Laravel validation?

No.

Laravel validation remains part of your Laravel application.

The package is designed to work with Laravel rather than introduce a completely separate validation system.

Which frontend frameworks can I use?

Laravel Inertia Forms is designed to support:

  • Vue
  • React
  • Svelte

This means your backend form definitions can remain consistent while the frontend implementation changes.

Can I create custom fields?

Yes.

Custom fields are important because every application eventually has requirements that cannot be covered by generic components.

You can extend the form system for project-specific use cases.

Can I use it for edit forms?

Yes.

Model binding makes it possible to work with existing model data, which makes the package useful for both create and edit workflows.

Does it support file uploads?

Yes.

File upload fields can be part of the same form structure instead of requiring a completely separate approach.

Can I build multi-step forms?

Yes.

Multi-step forms are useful for onboarding, applications, registration flows, checkout processes, and other larger workflows.

Is it useful for small projects?

It can be, but the biggest benefits appear in applications with many forms.

A standardized form architecture becomes increasingly valuable as the project grows.

Final Thoughts

Forms are one of the most common parts of web development.

They are also one of the easiest places for repetitive code to accumulate.

Laravel already gives us excellent tools for validation, authorization, models, requests, and backend business logic.

Inertia gives us a clean bridge between Laravel and modern frontend frameworks.

Laravel Inertia Forms brings those pieces together with a structured approach to form building.

Define your form once in PHP.

Keep Laravel responsible for validation and business rules.

Let Vue, React, or Svelte handle the presentation.

And spend less time rebuilding the same form infrastructure again and again.

Em um mundo onde as crianças passam horas presas a celulares e redes sociais, qual o verdadeiro papel do movimento e do esporte no desenvolvimento delas? Para aprofundar nesse tema, conversei com a pediatra Dra. Flávia de Oliveira, parceira de longa data da Bibi Calçados.

Dra. Flávia explicou que o principal problema das telas não é a tecnologia em si, mas o tempo que ela “rouba” de outras atividades essenciais para o desenvolvimento, como a prática de esportes, brincadeiras e interações sociais. Segundo ela, o uso da tecnologia deveria ser como um remédio: com dose e frequência corretas. Ela destacou a importância da “corporificação”, o processo pelo qual o cérebro precisa do movimento do corpo para se desenvolver plenamente. Quando o corpo não se mexe, o desenvolvimento cerebral fica prejudicado.

A pediatra compartilhou casos de seu consultório, como o de uma adolescente que chegou a passar nove horas por dia em frente à tela, a maior parte no TikTok. Ela reforça que a solução passa por uma “etiqueta digital” familiar, onde os pais dão o exemplo e estabelecem regras claras. A recomendação ideal, segundo especialistas, seria que crianças tivessem o primeiro celular apenas aos 14 ou 15 anos, e acesso a redes sociais aos 16.

Para a Dra. Flávia, o esporte é uma “ferramenta poderosíssima” na construção do ser humano. Através dele, a criança aprende a trabalhar o corpo, a conhecer seus limites, a lidar com a frustração de não conseguir algo e a sentir a conquista ao superar desafios, lições que se aplicam a todos os outros aspectos da vida.
